      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/id-porten-har-problemer-etter-dataangrep-1.18086360</link>
      <description>Innloggingstjenesten ID-porten har problemer.
Det bekrefter kommunikasjonsrådgiver Sara Neziri overfor NRK:
– Det er et pågående DDOs-angrep som gir noe ustabilitet i innlogging til ID-porten.
– Det kan påvirke Min ID, indirekte.
– Det jobbes aktivt med å få ID-porten helt stabil igjen, sier Neziri.

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/saudi-arabia_-har-skutt-ned-houthi-missiler-1.18086194</link>
      <description>Tre missiler som hadde retning mot Saudi-Arabias hovedstad Riyadh er skutt ned.
Det sier den saudiledede militærkoalisjonen, som en i pågående væpnet konflikt med houthi-militsen.
I tillegg skal det vært hørt flere eksplosjoner i Riyadh, melder Reuters.
Saudi-Arabia gikk til krig mot houthi-militsen i Jemen i 2015. Etter sju år med krig avtalte partene en våpenhvile i 2022.
I sommer har konflikten blusset opp igjen.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/historisk-_gta-6_-lansering_-solgte-for-nesten-4-milliarder-dollar-pa-en-dag-1.18086187</link>
      <description>Spillgiganten Rockstar Games knuser alle rekorder, melder Variety.
Allerede på lanseringsdagen omsatte «Grand Theft Auto 6», også kjent som «GTA 6», for 3,79 milliarder dollar.
Det tilsvarer over 37 milliarder norske kroner, og spillet forbigår dermed superheltfilmen «Avengers: End Game» som den største underholdningslanseringen noensinne.
«GTA 6» ble lansert torsdag på PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X og S, i tillegg til at det kan strømmes på Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming.
I den sjette utgaven av actionspillet følger spillerne duoen Jason og Lucia mens de ufører ran og andre kriminelle oppdrag i den fiktive amerikanske delstaten Leonida.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Israel med ny offensiv – tre drept</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/israel-med-ny-offensiv-_-tre-drept-1.18084431</link>
      <description>Israels hær sier den har innledet en operasjon i Hamas-kontrollerte områder i Gaza
Israel har innledet en militæroperasjon i det sentrale Gaza vest for den såkalte gule linjen, som har skilt Hamas-kontrollerte og israelsk-kontrollerte områder siden våpenhvilen trådte i kraft i fjor. Det opplyser militæret til AFP.
Vitner sier at israelske stridsvogner rullet inn på hovedveien Salahudeen, vest for den såkalte gule linjen som markerer grensen for de to tredjedelene av Gazastripen som fortsatt er under israelsk kontroll.
Den såkalte gule linjen ble etablert etter våpenhvilen i oktober 2025 og skiller israelskkontrollerte og palestinske soner i Gazastripen. Israelske styrker har gradvis flyttet den gule linjen og utvidet området under direkte militær kontroll i Gaza.</description>

Electric vehicle drivers have a new fast-charging option in Brentwood Bay, where half a dozen drivers can power up at the same time.

Installed at the Heritage School Museum, located at 7130 West Saanich Road, the station has three 180-kilowatt chargers, with room for six EVs to charge at once.

In 10 minutes, one 180-kilowatt charge provides vehicles with an additional 180 kilometres of driving. 

“Through power-sharing technology, each unit can serve two vehicles at once by splitting its output. For example, a 180-kilowatt charger can supply two vehicles with 90 kilowatts each. This allows up to six EVs to use the chargers simultaneously,” states BC Hydro in its release.

With the addition of the new Brentwood Bay station, BC Hydro has eight EV charging sites across Greater Victoria, amounting to a combined total of 57 charging ports for drivers.

In late September, BC Hydro announced a new fast-charging site in Esquimalt. The site features a similar arrangement, providing room for six, with three 180-kilowatt chargers.

Equipped with CCS, CHAdeMO and NACS connectors, the stations are able to power a wide range of electric vehicles.

The additional seven locations are listed below:

  • Sidney Beacon Plaza (2337 Beacon Avenue, Sidney)
  • Sidney Mary Winspear Centre (2304 Oakville Avenue, Sidney)
  • G.R. Pearkes Recreation Centre (3100 Tillicum Road, Saanich)
  • Saanich Plaza (3544 Blanshard Street, Saanich)
  • Victoria Downtown (1425 Store Street, Victoria)
  • Victoria Ogden Point Cruise Ship Terminals North and South (185 Dallas Road, Victoria)
  • Archie Browning Sports Centre (1151 Esquimalt Road, Esquimalt)

This summer, the province announced a $700 million plan to triple the number of charging ports across B.C. by 2035.

“BC Hydro’s public fast-charging network includes 917 charging ports at 190 locations in the province. As demand continues to grow, BC Hydro is accelerating expansion plans, targeting 3,500 ports by 2035,” stated the government release in July 2026.

Find more information about these charging stations at BC Hydro.

And it doesn’t stop there. The meat is served up with house-made coleslaw, signature sauces and Russ’s famous beans.

]]>

The message at the Victoria Sexual Assault Centre (VSAC) hasn’t changed much over four decades: It’s not your fault, help is available, and healing is possible.

These two women at the VSAC are at opposite ends of the spectrum. CEO Ashley Dryburgh has been here about three months, while Karen Wickham, VSAC clinic and access coordinator, started shortly after it opened in 1993.

Starting with a staff of three back then, now there are 30 permanent employees, 20 auxiliary staff and a dedicated group of highly trained volunteers who are completely committed to giving survivors, all survivors, what they need

“Anyone of any gender can experience sexualized violence and I’m so proud that we are a trans-inclusive organization,” said Karen.

Recognizing that Indigenous women and girls are particularly vulnerable, they’ve established an Indigenous response network as well.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

VSAC offers crisis support, counselling, forensic exams and outreach services. Staff here do as little or as much as the survivor wants.

“They can sit down and do some beading or just sit and be comfortable for a while,” said Ashley. “If they are just wanting medications that are commonly given after a sex assault, that’s all we’ll do. If they want their big toe looked at and that’s it, that’s all we’re going to do.”

But VSAC can do so much more.

“It provides hope, it provides healing, we provide education and connection and it ultimately makes our entire community a better, safer place to be for everybody,” said Karen.

And there is joy here as well.

“You have to balance the darkness with the light, and there isn’t a single day that goes by here where I don’t hear laughter in the corridors, where we aren’t trying to uplift each other,” said Ashley.

When asked if she ever felt like leaving, Karen said, “No.”

“It makes me feel very honoured that someone has allowed me to assist them as they’re going through their journey,” she said.

What has been created here is thoughtful, comfortable and safe. And this is the message:

“It’s not your fault, there is help available and healing is possible,” said Ashley.

Whether in the clinic room with a handmade quilt, in the healing room, even in the hallways adorned with gifted art from survivors and staff alike, the Victoria Sexual Assault Centre is here, still, after 40 years, to care for those who need it.

]]> 1362987 Woman in critical condition treated in Port Hardy parking lot, before dying https://cheknews.ca/woman-in-critical-condition-treated-in-port-hardy-parking-lot-before-dying-1363026/ Sat, 21 Nov 2026 02:40:36 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1363026

The post Woman in critical condition treated in Port Hardy parking lot, before dying appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

There are many questions and few answers after a woman in critical condition arrived at the Port Hardy hospital after it had closed for the night.

“Frankly, it’s been very upsetting,” said Dr. Alex Nataros, a family physician with North Island Community Health Centre.

Thursday night, a woman arrived at the Port Hardy Hospital after 5 p.m., when the emergency room was closed.

Instead of being seen inside by doctors, she was treated in the parking lot by paramedics.

Eventually she made it inside the hospital where she couldn’t be resuscitated and was pronounced dead.

For nearly four years, the Port Hardy’s emergency room closes at 5 p.m. due to reported health provider shortages.

Nataros says a fellow North Island doctor was doing their rounds with patients in the 18-bed community hospital Thursday night after 5 p.m., when tragedy struck outside.

“My colleague is obviously very shaken up that this person died,” said Nataros.

Nataros says paramedics were performing CPR outside “for a prolonged period of time.”

“That is unusual,” said Nataros, who doesn’t know why the woman wasn’t taken to the nearest open hospital in Port McNeill.

BC Emergency Health Services (BC EHS) says at 5:11 p.m. Thursday, a paramedic at the hospital “became aware that there was a patient in need of medical treatment in the hospital parking lot.”

“Two additional ambulances responded to the scene. Paramedics provided emergency medical treatment to the patient, who was transferred to the care of Port Hardy Hospital staff in critical condition,” said BC EHS in a statement.

Island Health says it’s reviewing the circumstances of the case with BC EHS.

The BC Coroners Service says it’s also investigating the death.

Nataros was suspended by Island Health in 2023 from working in its emergency rooms following patient and healthcare worker complaints raising patient safety concerns.

He has also been outspoken in his criticism of Island Health over staffing shortages and advocacy for reopening Port Hardy Hospital’s overnight emergency services, and sees the death as related to Port Hardy’s ongoing nightly emergency room closures.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

“There’s been deaths, and too many deaths,” said Nataros. “It’s unacceptable. It’s reprehensible that our emergency has been closed for almost four years.

“I’m hopeful that the new Minister of Health Ryan Peterson, as well as our North Island MLA Anna Kindy in her new role as Minister of State for Rural Issues, will address this urgently and get Port Hardy emerge open as the primary emerge for the North Island.”

Peterson and Kindy were unable to comment Friday as they were only sworn into their new cabinet roles today, however, Kindy has previously been outspoken on the issue, as has B.C.’s Premier Lorne Doerkson.

“We will reverse ER closures and increase rural health care access,” promised Doerkson on October 5th, speaking outside 100 Mile House’s hospital.

“To support this, we will create a $50 million emergency fund which will be available for rural medical practices to prevent closures and aid recruitment.”

]]> 1363026 Remembering Terry Wilson, Fernwood’s beloved Bubble Man https://cheknews.ca/remembering-terry-wilson-fernwoods-beloved-bubble-man-1363094/ Sat, 21 Nov 2026 02:33:06 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1363094

]]>

You might not know the name Terry Wilson, but if you’ve spent a lot of time in Fernwood, you know Terry the Bubble Man.

He was the guy in Fernwood Square in curious clothes, blowing massive bubbles into the air for, and occasionally at strangers. Whatever it took to get a smile.

And he did it for decades.

Terry the Bubble Man died recently at the age of 82, leaving a noticeable absence in a neighbourhood where he had become something of an institution.

The news prompted an outpouring of memories on Reddit, with people sharing stories of childhood encounters, chance conversations and the simple comfort of knowing Terry was around.

“He kinda dressed like a wizard,” said Victoria City Coun. Jeremy Caradonna at Wilson’s daily coffee stop, Little June.

For some, Terry was part of growing up in Fernwood.

Soli, who lived about a block away from the square, remembers chasing and popping hundreds of his bubbles as a kid.

“It was always nice to see him around, even if I wasn’t chatting with him, just kind of knowing he’s still there,” Soli said.

At Little June, staff knew Terry by name and his order by heart.

“Espresso. Terry always got an espresso,” said Jacqueline.

While thousands of people may have crossed paths with Terry over the years, not everyone knew much about the man behind the bubbles.

Graham Benesch did. The two were neighbours for 35 years, and Benesch says he last saw Terry just two days before his death.

He remembers a man who quietly looked out for the people around him.

When it snowed, Benesch says, Terry would sometimes shovel the walkway outside his building without anyone knowing who had done it.

“That man would go out of his way to help you. Without you even knowing,” Benesch said. “It’s a huge loss for Fernwood. A huge loss for Victoria.”

Terry’s outlook on life was captured in a 2013 Shaw TV interview, when he talked about the importance of holding onto a sense of childhood wonder.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

“It’s important not to let the kid part of us go as we get older,” Terry said.

It’s a sentiment that seems to have resonated with a lot of people in Fernwood.

Caradonna is bringing a motion to Victoria city council to explore a small memorial in Terry’s honour. Ideas include a plaque, a bench or perhaps some kind of permanent bubble installation.

Terry didn’t leave behind any known wishes for a memorial. But the neighbourhood he called home is already thinking about how to remember him.

For Benesch, the reason people connected with Terry was simple.

“He just wanted to see people smile.”

And for a man who spent so many years putting bubbles into the Fernwood sky, that’s not a bad legacy to leave behind.

The Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation is launching an ambitious new fundraising campaign focused on robotics.

Its goal is to raise $3.5 million to launch the first surgical robotics program at a hospital north of the Malahat.

As you enter Nanaimo Regional General Hospital’s property from Dufferin Street, you’ll see the new billboard that went up Thursday.

The Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation wants to purchase the da Vinci Surgical System.

“It’s the new standard of care for doing surgeries, especially in urology. All the new fellowship-trained graduates, they need this equipment to do the surgeries that we currently do. They can do them better. They can do them in tighter spots. They can lead to better recoveries, quicker recoveries for the patients,” said Dr. Will Carlson, a urologist at
NRGH.

The robotic system allows surgeons to operate with enhanced precision, visualization and control through smaller incisions, including in areas of the body that would otherwise be difficult to reach.

It comes as a new cancer centre at the hospital gets closer to reality every day. Planning is also underway for a new patient tower and cardiovascular intervention centre.

“That we’ve gotten to a place where we can actually have surgical robotics here on central Vancouver Island, we’re really excited about that. It came to Victoria two years ago. Of course it’s been in Vancouver for almost 20 years so we’re really catching up to where our community needs to be,” said Barney Ellis-Perry, the CEO of Nanaimo & District Hospital Foundation.

Both Royal Jubilee and Victoria General hospitals have them after a similar campaign in greater Victoria.

One Campbell River-born doctor is already training on the system, believing the campaign will be successful.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

“He has options to go to bigger, fancier places but he wants to come here and take care of the people of Nanaimo and the central island so he’ll be starting with us in August and we’re super excited and he can’t do the surgery that he’s trained to do without this piece of equipment,” said Carlson.

Ellis-Perry says he’s always nervous to see if enough donors will actually step up but he always ends up being amazed.

“I’m blown away every time you get the call you’re not expecting. I really believe in this. My partner was affected. The idea of a dedicated Mount Washington fire department was first talked about back in 1979 but it took several high-profile chalet fires to get residents and politicians talking about it and voting to go ahead with it.

“It was 1979 when the concept was first floated,” said retired regional district Area C director Edwin Grieve.

Now, the doors are finally open on a $2.5 million fire hall where the former Vancouver Island Mountain Centre once operated near Raven Lodge.

“It’s what the residents need and I think this will greatly enhance fire protection up here because we have equipment up here year-round now,” Oyster River Fire Chief Bruce Green told CHEK News Friday.

A new two-bay building was built to house the fire apparatus while the former sports training centre will be used for office space and community rentals.

The Oyster River Fire Department assumed responsibility for fire protection on the mountain in 2018 but worked out of a sea can and the lone fire truck could only be stationed there in the summer months.

An ATV on tracks was the responding vehicle during winter months.

The department saved neighbouring chalets when a fire broke out in March 2020, thanks to the volunteers who live on the mountain, and the ATV that transported crews to the scene with hoses and gear.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

Fire hydrants had already been installed in the village but there was no fire department to use them.

Ten volunteers, people who live full or part-time in the village will now respond out of the new hall.

“Oh it’s incredible. To know that we have a base to work out of, especially on days that it’s snowy, the road closes down, it’s very reassuring for us to feel like we can provide services to the community,” said volunteer firefighter Heidi Fuerste.

“Well it’s a great benefit to the mountain community, now we can have quicker response times,” added Chris Hounsell, who also lives on the mountain part-time.

Property owners are relieved to finally have a local fire hall, after a referendum was held in 2016.

“Well it’s important for insurance purposes, important for people who lose their places because there isn’t adequate fire protection and it will bring the community together,” said Bill Jackson who owns a condominium in the resort.

Retired regional district director Edwin Grieve says it was a huge fire that destroyed three chalets on Fosters Place in 2015 that really got people talking again.

“And luckily there were no injuries, nobody was hurt,” Grieve said. “The fire that took out three chalets in one fell swoop and I think that was the clincher.”

Chief Bruce Green says response time for fires, medical calls and crashes on Strathcona Parkway will be a lot faster and help will still come from fire halls in Oyster River and Merville.

Gatherings are taking place across Canada Friday for Transgender Day of Remembrance, including a rally in the capital, just hours after the swearing-in of new Premier Lorne Doerkson and his B.C. Conservative cabinet, prompting concerns from advocacy groups about policy shifts.

In Victoria, groups were scheduled to meet outside the B.C. Legislature at 4 p.m. to recognize ongoing violence and elevated risks facing transgender, nonbinary, Two-Spirit, and gender diverse and gender-variant people whose lives have been lost due to transgender violence.

Statistics Canada finds transgender and non-binary populations face a disproportionately higher risk of violence compared to cisgender men and women.

In 2025, 148 women and girls were killed by violence, according to a study by Women and Gender Equality Canada.

On Sept. 28, 2026, Doerkson said, “I firmly believe that we have to repeal SOGI”. Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity is anti-bullying curriculum introduced by the former B.C. NDP government in 2016-2017. Doerkson said it had become a source of division in the province, while stating schools must remain safe for children. 

The Public Service Alliance of Canada criticized the pledge to remove SOGI 123 resources, citing a B.C. member survey where half of trans and gender-diverse respondents reported workplace discrimination, harassment, or racism. 

In 2017, the former B.C. NDP Government noted studies showing SOGI policies improve school climates and reduce discrimination and suicide attempts for all students.

On Friday, the BC Greens expressed disappointment over Caroline Elliott’s appointment as Attorney General on Transgender Day of Remembrance, citing Elliot’s past suggestion to use the Notwithstanding Clause regarding trans rights and raising concerns for Indigenous and provincial human rights.

Gender-based violence in Canada

In the past year, gender diverse people were nearly four times as likely as cisgender people to experience violence—76 per cent compared to 32 per cent over the past year, according to Statistics Canada.

In response to this, Federal Minister Rechie Valdez said Friday, “These numbers are a stark reminder of the barriers too many Canadians continue to face simply for being who they are.” 

Valedz, minister of women and gender equality and secretary of state for small business and tourism, pointed to the ministry’s plans to support safer spaces for gender diverse people through its proposed 2026 federal budget.

The ministry plans to fund 2SLGBTQI+ community projects with $60 million over four years and $15 million each year after.

In Canada, transgender and non-binary people experience higher rates of physical and sexual assault than cisgender people:

  • Physical assault: Affected 13% of transgender men, 12% of non-binary people, and 8.7% of transgender women, compared to 3.6% of cisgender men and 2.5% of cisgender women.
  • Sexual assault: Affected 7% of non-binary people, 6.3% of transgender women, and 5.9% of transgender men, compared to 2.3% of cisgender women and 0.8% of cisgender men.

Unwanted online behaviour targeted three times as many gender-diverse individuals as cisgender people in 2025, a heightened risk that persists across all age groups according to StatsCan. 

And the range of online violence—such as harassment, cyberstalking, and non-consensual sharing of explicit material—was linked to higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation and attempts among 2SLGBTQ+ people.

Advocacy groups are working to create safer spaces to protect gender diverse populations 

Advocacy groups remain cautious as the new provincial government takes office.

In November 2026, a B.C. Human Rights Tribunal ruling highlights a recent case of workplace discrimination in B.C. The tribunal ordered LifeLabs LP to pay $32,000 for injury to dignity—plus lost wages and expert report costs—over incidents involving transgender and non-binary Lower Mainland patients that caused them to avoid medical care in 2019.

The ruling addresses incidents where LifeLabs refused services based on the individual’s expressed non-binary gender identity, and in front of other patients, required them to pick a binary gender that did not match their identity.

Statistics Canada says there’s been a national decline in people being free to express their gender identity of choosing. Between 2018 and 2025, gender expression for both men and women dropped across the country by eight percentage points.

Across the report on gender-based violence, gender expression had the largest shift in findings. But, a recent study finds that support and acceptance can save lives.

The 2025 Journal of Adolescent Health study cited fewer suicide attempts among LGBTQ+ youth who were supported and accepted by parents and caregivers, highlighting the need for culturally competent support and policies across diverse families.

In addition to Friday’s rally, UVSS Pride and the Gender Empowerment Centre has provided a list of online resources and urges people to support gender-diverse peers by speaking against hateful speech, respecting pronouns, staying informed through trans media, advocating for medical care, housing and hiring trans people, and opposing discriminatory legislation. 

The rally for Trans Day of Remembrance takes place from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. at the BC Legislature.

“BC Transit has shown its true colours twice this week. First, it caused widespread anxiety among riders with a false strike announcement. Now, it is doubling down on making riders and frontline workers do more with less,” said Unifor Local 333-BC president Stephen Bains. 

“When the buses stop on Friday, November 27, we hope BC Transit remembers who keeps them moving and why we keep them moving.”

Unifor Local 333-BC  represents nearly 800 workers, including transit operators and mechanics at BC Transit in Greater Victoria.

The union’s collective agreement expired on March 31, 2025 and job action has been escalating since August.
